paragraph.text: B11. "Live animal transport is regulated and follows standards to ensure the animals' welfare"

there are standards, but they allow very long journeys and are poorly enforced. In the European Union, a bovine can travel 14 hours, rest 1 and travel another 14; the European scientific authority points to heat, injuries, hunger, thirst and lack of space as core problems on these journeys, and there are documented cases of animals amid accumulated feces and urine. A European Parliament committee of inquiry concluded in 2021 that the rules were repeatedly breached in member states. Australia passed a law in 2024 ending live sheep exports by sea from 2028, recognizing that rules weren't solving the problem. And even when fully followed, the standards regulate the journey of an animal who will be killed at the destination.

some activists think NGOs spend too much time and money on reforms, such as transport rules, that don't end exploitation; others see them as a real reduction in suffering and a step toward bigger changes. The discussion remains open
"Animal transport is regulated, there are rules for everything: journey time, water, rest. They exist to ensure the animals' welfare."
There are laws regulating live animal transport: journey time, space, water, food and rest.
These laws are based on technical knowledge about animal welfare.
If the journey follows technical standards, the animal doesn't suffer significantly.
So live animal transport is acceptable.
P1 is true in many countries. P2 is partly true. P3 fails twice: the standards allow long, stressful journeys, and they are often not followed.
"There are rules for everything, even journey times."
"The law sets stocking densities, maximum journey times and rest stops."
"The law guarantees animal welfare." (which is B10)

Imagine spending a whole day in a crowded truck, not understanding where you're going, hot or cold, sometimes without water and in the middle of your own mess. There are rules for these journeys, but they allow the journey to be very long, and they aren't always followed. And at the end of the journey, the animal goes to the slaughterhouse.

There are standards, yes, but do you know what they allow? In the European Union, a bovine can travel 14 hours, rest 1 and travel another 14, with heat, injuries, thirst and little space. And they are poorly enforced: a European Parliament committee of inquiry concluded in 2021 that they were repeatedly breached. Australia decided to end live sheep exports by sea from 2028, because rules weren't solving the problem. And even when followed, the standards regulate the journey of an animal who will be killed at the destination.
"If the standards solved the problem, why did a country decide to ban live sheep exports by sea altogether?"
The argument treats the existence of a standard as proof that the problem is solved:
How long can the animal travel?
In the EU, cattle can travel 14 hours, rest 1 and travel another 14; pigs, up to 24 hours with access to water
Heat, injuries, thirst and little space; in documented cases, accumulated feces and urine
The European Parliament found repeated breaches and no Commission proceedings against the countries
Australia decided to ban sheep exports by sea

EU Regulation 1/2005, one of the most detailed in the world, lets cattle travel 14 hours, rest 1 hour and travel another 14, and pigs travel up to 24 hours with access to water. In 2022, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recommended shorter journeys, more space and temperature limits inside vehicles.

text.bold: 2. Conditions on the journey are harsh, even within the rules.

paragraph.text: In its 2022 opinion on cattle, EFSA listed eleven highly relevant welfare consequences of transport, including heat stress, injuries, restriction of movement, prolonged hunger and thirst, and resting problems. According to the opinion, severe heat stress begins at around 25 °C inside the vehicle, thirst can set in after 9 hours even with drinkers, and more space than currently allowed would reduce falls and injuries. When enforcement fails, sanitary conditions get worse. In 2018, at the port of Santos, Brazil, a court-appointed veterinarian described the "immense quantity of urine and excrement" accumulated on the ship

, which was carrying around 27,000 cattle to Turkey, and the federal judge in the case found hygiene "very precarious". Inspectors from Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture said they found no mistreatment, and the ruling was overturned on appeal. In a separate case, about the trucking of these cattle to the port, a Santos court in 2023 ordered the exporter, at first instance, to pay BRL 1.39 million in collective moral damages; according to the public prosecutor, the animals traveled packed tightly, without proper ventilation or hygiene, for long periods.

The European Parliament's committee of inquiry on the protection of animals during transport concluded in 2021 that the regulation was not consistently complied with in member states, and that the European Commission had opened no infringement proceedings against any country despite repeated violations.

text.bold: 4. Some problems can't be fixed with rules.

paragraph.text: After mass deaths on ships, Australia passed a law in 2024 banning live sheep exports by sea from 1 May 2028. Cattle and goats are still exported.
In December 2023, the European Commission proposed a new regulation, with a 9-hour limit for journeys to slaughter. The proposal received thousands of amendments, and negotiations stalled.
Even a perfect journey ends at the slaughterhouse. The standard regulates how the animal arrives at its death, not whether it should die (B1).

(d) The strongest counter-reply: standards improve over time

The most serious version acknowledges the failures and says the standards are being revised, that welfare science guides those revisions, and that the way forward is better enforcement, not condemning transport itself.

Even the most ambitious proposals keep journeys of many hours and slaughter at the destination.

It's true that there are standards, that some were based on welfare science, and that they prevent some of the worst abuses. It's also true that improving transport reduces real suffering, and many organizations devote effort to it.

Some activists think NGOs spend too much time and money on reforms of this kind, which don't end exploitation; others see them as a real reduction in suffering and a step toward bigger changes. The discussion remains open. What isn't open is that the standard, however good, regulates the journey of an animal who will be killed at the end.
